source.title: Tradeoffs Between Alignment and Helpfulness in Language Models
source.authors: Yotam Wolf; Noam Wies; Dorin Shteyman; Binyamin Rothberg; Yoav Levine; A. Shashua

record.tranche_reason: The study uses PCA-based representation steering rather than the original difference-in-means direction and tests its effects on harmful-request behavior and general capability. It does not perform the original ablation.
record.gate_note: The study measures behavior after adding steering vectors and reports helpfulness under the same intervention. Its vector constructions, layer choices, and theoretical assumptions are not experimental outcomes and are not rows. Racism and bias results are omitted because they do not measure refusal or another behavior named by the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study builds PCA steering vectors from harmful vs. unharmful instruction contrasts (Llama 2 13B chat) and from aligned vs. misaligned responses (Llama 2 13B base). It adds them at layers -25 to -33 and measures the rate of refusing vs. fulfilling 100 AdvBench requests, plus MMLU and HumanEval under the same vectors. This bears on V1's addition and capability-retention parts by a different method: PCA rather than difference-in-means, addition only, no ablation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors prove, and show empirically, that steering raises alignment roughly linearly in vector norm (tanh bound) while helpfulness falls quadratically near zero. Large norms can guarantee alignment at a capability cost; small norms such as re about 2.5 give an efficient regime.
record.recipe_differences: Uses PCA over paired positive/negative behavior-prompt representation differences, not the original difference-in-means direction. It adds vectors at selected layers (layers −11 to −30 for bias and −25 to −33 for harmfulness/harmlessness), and does not ablate the direction or intervene at every position.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports different vector constructions and injection-layer ranges for bias versus harmfulness/harmlessness. Its behavior and capability outcomes are measured over coefficient sweeps; no further prompt- or judge-specific sensitivity is described for refusal.
record.peer_reviewed: ICLR 2025 Workshop on Foundation Models in the Wild
record.problems: The refusal-related intervention is not an ablation and does not use the exact claimed direction; vectors are injected only in selected layers. Several model- and condition-specific outcomes are only shown in figures, without textual values. The paper's theory relies on stated assumptions about classification and random effects on unrelated answers.
record.rows_left_out: No results bearing on the claim were omitted for the 60-row limit. Bias/racism behavior outcomes were not included because the claim versions concern refusal and harmfulness rather than those behaviors.

untested.parts: Directional ablation; the exact difference-in-means direction; intervention at all layers and positions; inducing refusal on harmless requests in an aligned chat model by adding the direction.
All: no jailbreak mechanism or adversarial-training test.
All: only the first PC is used; no multi-direction comparison.
All: vectors built per model; no transfer test.
All: base and chat models get differently constructed vectors, so they are not compared on whether one removable direction exists.

missing.what: Helpfulness under harm/harmless vectors measured over the full vocabulary (sampled answers) and as accuracy for Llama 2 13B and 13B chat; reported as similar to Fig. 5.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's focus is a general alignment/helpfulness tradeoff theory. The refusal-relevant evidence is a few figure-level results on Llama 2 13B, and the Llama 3.1 results are figure only. The Fig. 4a caption conflicts with Appendix F.2 on which vector was used for the base model.

versions.untested_parts: No ablation; no test of the exact harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means direction; vectors are PCA-derived and applied only to selected layers, not every layer and position. The study does not test refusal of harmless requests. It measures harmful-request behavior and selected capability benchmarks.
No test of attacks suppressing the direction or training against its ablation.
No comparison of a single direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
Vectors are constructed separately for models; no cross-language or cross-model transfer test.
The study uses pretrained and chat/instruct models but does not manipulate refusal training or test whether training determines the existence of a removable direction.

rows.subject: Llama 2 13B
rows.operation_detail: Injected harmlessness PCA representation-engineering vectors while evaluating responses to harmful instructions.

conditions.value: sweep; text states re = 2.5 suffices for a significant change

rows.measure: Harmful-behavior expectation, based on whether the response fulfills or refuses a harmful instruction.
rows.baseline: Negative behavior expectation without steering, as described for the tested behavior sweep.
rows.value: The expectation changes from negative to positive; text states re = 2.5 suffices for a significant change. Per-coefficient values are figure only.
rows.uncertainty: not stated
rows.note: The paper describes this as aligning the pretrained model toward harmless behavior. This is not a test of the original ablation or exact difference-in-means direction.
rows.check: Per Appendix F.2 the vector is a harmlessness vector built from aligned vs. misaligned responses to harmful instructions, not harmful-minus-harmless instructions. The Fig. 4a caption saying 'harmful PCA vectors' appears to be a typo. Subject is a base (pretrained) model, so this shows refusal induced by addition in a non-chat model, not the original setting.

rows.subject: Llama 2 13B chat
rows.operation_detail: Injected harmfulness PCA representation-engineering vectors while evaluating responses to harmful instructions.

conditions.value: sweep; text states re = 2.5 suffices for a significant change

rows.measure: Harmful-behavior expectation, based on whether the response fulfills or refuses a harmful instruction.
rows.baseline: Negative behavior expectation without steering, as described for the tested behavior sweep.
rows.value: The expectation changes from negative to positive; text states re = 2.5 suffices for a significant change. Per-coefficient values are figure only.
rows.uncertainty: not stated
rows.note: The direction is used to misalign the aligned chat model, increasing harmful compliance. This does not test removal of the claimed direction.
rows.check: Closest to V1: the vector is PCA of harmful (AdvBench) minus unharmful (shareGPT) instruction representations, added toward 'harmful'. This suppresses refusal, the opposite sign of V1's 'adding induces refusal'; it is not ablation. The baseline should read: chat model's negative behavior expectation, i.e. mostly refuses, at re=0.

relationships.condition: Llama 2 13B chat; PCA vector of harmful vs. unharmful instructions added at layers -25 to -33; AdvBench, 100 prompts
relationships.reason: At re=2.5 behavior expectation flips from refusing to complying, so one contrast direction controls refusal (B2).
relationships.display_finding: At re=2.5, expected behavior switched from refusal to compliance.

relationships.condition: Llama 2 13B base; harmlessness vector from aligned vs. misaligned responses
relationships.reason: Adding the vector moves the base model from complying to refusing harmful requests by re=2.5 (B1). The vector construction differs from V1's.
relationships.display_finding: Adding a harmlessness vector derived from aligned versus misaligned responses changed the base model from compliance to refusal by re=2.5.

relationships.condition: Capability under the same harm/harmless vectors, Llama 2 13B and 13B chat (MMLU, HumanEval)
relationships.reason: MMLU correct-answer probability and HumanEval peak at re=0 and decay roughly quadratically. The loss is small at re=2.5 but grows with steering strength, so ability retention depends on the coefficient (M1-M3, M7-M9, C1).
relationships.display_finding: MMLU correct-answer probability and HumanEval peaked at re=0 and declined roughly quadratically, with small losses at re=2.5 and larger losses under stronger steering.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Llama 2 13B pretrained model; harmlessness steering on harmful AdvBench requests
reader_labels.reason: Adding the steering vectors shifts harmful-behavior expectation from negative to positive, consistent with a causal effect on refusal behavior (B1). This supports only a related steering effect, not the exact direction or intervention in V1.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Capability measurements under steering; Llama 2 13B and Llama 2 13B chat
reader_labels.reason: The reported MMLU and HumanEval trends show capability declining as steering grows, although the text describes the MMLU decrease at re = 2.5 as not too great (M1-M12, C1-C2). The study does not establish that abilities remain largely intact across settings.
